A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. v2 Appendices A–D correspond to v3 Appendices B–E; v3 additionally introduces an explanatory Appendix A. The material supports a reliable comparison.

before.justification: Sections 5–6 and Appendix D report original experiments comparing counterfactual explanations and evaluating learned generators on healthcare-derived and synthetic datasets.

after.justification: Sections 5–6 and Appendix E retain original experimental results, including generator accuracy, fairness comparisons, sensitivity analyses, and data-augmentation outcomes.

M1.justification: The optimization formulations, neural-network architectures and losses, Hamming-distance generator, and Algorithm 1 augmentation procedure are retained. The additional explanations and proposed future extensions do not change the implemented methods.

E1.justification: Healthcare-derived BMI, WHR, and BRFSS coverage and the synthetic dimensionality, information-access, feature-eligibility, and action-restriction scenarios are retained. v3 replaces the introductory '11+' counts with 30 semi-synthetic and 34 synthetic datasets; these variants were already described in v2 Appendix A.

E2.justification: The reported comparisons retain Ustun et al.'s low-level recourse generator, the Hamming-distance baseline, and the same high-level generators. The newly discussed global recourse methods are cited and contextualized but are not added to the experimental comparisons.

E3.justification: The 80/20 splits, model settings, exact-match evaluation, and comparison metrics are retained. v3 newly documents validation and tie handling without reporting a change to the existing experiments. Removing 'average' from some metric descriptions clarifies the already defined per-agent differences.

E4.justification: The dimensionality, CFE-frequency, augmentation, model-complexity, restricted-action, feature-eligibility, and error analyses are retained. New Figure 11 redisplays the existing WHR difference analysis. Model-drift investigations and user studies are proposed future work, not additional evaluations.

E5.justification: The accuracy tables retain their uncertainty entries, and Kendall tau, p-value, and dispersion reporting are unchanged. v3 introduces no repeated-run counts, seeds, or new uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: All six tables have identical entries. For example, BMI hl-continuous accuracy remains 0.92 ± 0.0053, and 100-dimensional accuracy after AG2 remains 0.790 ± 0.00565. Corresponding findings and plots are retained; new Figure 11 provides another display of the existing WHR differences.

T1.justification: Definitions 1–2 and Equations 1–13 retain their mathematical content. The explicit state-space notation and new appendix explanations clarify existing concepts without adding a theorem, proof, substantive formal assumption, or derivation.

C1.justification: The three recourse types, single-agent formulations, learned generators, and headline accuracy, efficiency, and recourse advantages remain the core contributions. The expanded abstract explicitly identifies classifier types and synthetic evaluations already present in v2.

C2.justification: Section 7 and new Appendix C.4 substantially expand the limitations discussion to cover linear-classifier dependence, classifier errors and drift, and the strictness of exact-match evaluation for valid but costlier CFEs. Appendix A discusses applicability and adaptation challenges, while Appendix E.4.2 identifies user studies as needed to validate interpretability claims.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies GridSearchCV for classifier tuning, validation_split during generator training, and exclusion of agents with tied minimum-cost CFEs. The introduction's code link changes from an anonymous review repository to the named ripl/LAR-LSS GitHub repository. These are documentation and access-information changes.

R1.justification: Sections 2 and 8 replace the blanket characterization of low-level generators as single-agent methods with discussion of global recourse work by Pedapati, Rawal and Lakkaraju, Kanamori, Ley, and Carrizosa. The detailed positioning against Counterfactual Explanation Trees substantially revises the prior-work comparison. Robustness and classifier-approximation literature are also added.

P1.justification: v3 revises the abstract and several explanatory paragraphs, expands related work, and adds explanatory appendix sections. Author and publication-header text also change. The original main-section sequence and most existing prose and appendix organization remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figure 11 with two per-agent WHR difference plots, refines labels and captions in Figures 3 and 10, and relocates or renumbers subsequent material. Publication headers and the title-page author layout change. Existing table structures and embedded example images are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 improves research positioning by acknowledging global recourse methods, clarifies important applicability and evaluation limitations, and discloses validation, tie handling, and a named code repository. These address specific gaps in contextualization and reproducibility. The overall gain is limited to clearer qualification and documentation of an unchanged methodological and empirical contribution.
